country.name: Brazil
country.kicker: A continent’s scale. A world’s living systems.

overview.summary: South America’s largest country is an urban, Portuguese-speaking society with extraordinary ecological reach. Its farms, forests, and cities place it at the heart of debates about development and the planet.
overview.geography: Brazil spans much of eastern South America and faces the Atlantic. The Amazon lies mostly in the north; many of the largest population centers sit nearer the eastern and southeastern coast.

whyItMatters.title: An ecosystem with global consequences
whyItMatters.text: The Amazon stores carbon, sustains exceptional biodiversity, and moves moisture across a vast region.

whyItMatters.title: A major link in the world’s food supply
whyItMatters.text: Soy, coffee, sugar, and meat connect Brazil’s land-use choices to dinner tables and markets far away.

stories.question: Why does the Amazon matter beyond Brazil?
stories.summary: A forest is also part of the atmosphere’s plumbing.

sections.title: Water on the move
sections.text: Trees release moisture into the air. The Amazon’s water cycle helps shape rainfall across parts of South America, alongside its role in carbon storage and biodiversity.

sections.title: A shared system
sections.text: The Amazon crosses national borders. Forest loss, fire, farming, and infrastructure affect ecosystems and the people who depend on them, including Indigenous communities.

stories.takeaway: Protecting the Amazon is also about water, livelihoods, and decisions made far from the forest.

scene.mapNote: The Amazon Basin extends into several neighboring countries.

stories.question: Why does Brazil speak Portuguese?
stories.summary: A colonial past left a different linguistic map from most of South America.

sections.title: A Portuguese colony
sections.text: Portuguese colonization, beginning in 1500, imposed a language and institutions over a land already home to diverse Indigenous peoples.

sections.title: A society formed through unequal encounters
sections.text: Enslaved Africans and their descendants profoundly shaped Brazil. Independence in 1822 did not end slavery, which continued until 1888. Indigenous languages and migrant traditions persist alongside Portuguese.

stories.takeaway: A shared official language sits on top of many histories, including histories of violence and resistance.

scene.mapNote: The Atlantic connected colonial Brazil with Portugal and West Africa.

stories.question: How did Brazil become an agricultural giant?
stories.summary: This is not just a story about abundant land.

sections.title: A transformed interior
sections.text: Research, infrastructure, credit, and new farming techniques helped expand production, including in the Cerrado savanna.

sections.title: The trade-off on the ground
sections.text: Agriculture supports exports and employment. Expansion can also put pressure on habitats, water, and land rights. The Cerrado and the Amazon are distinct ecosystems.

stories.takeaway: The question is not simply how much Brazil produces, but where and how it produces it.

scene.mapNote: The Cerrado lies largely south and east of the Amazon.
